sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. Others like to look at a page or two before moving on to something else. Keep the book out — kids might want to return to it later, which you should encourage. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... Keep active hands busy with lift-the-flap pages and textures to feel. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... It's OK if your child can't sit still for an entire book — toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon. ... Choose books with many pictures that your child can point to and name.
sources.supports: Busy toddlers may stand or move while a parent reads, a child who does not look can still be listening, repeating a favourite book, a basket of books on the floor and choosing from a few, a regular time before naps and bedtime, flaps and textures for busy hands, putting the book aside when it turns tense, attention spans growing, and books with many pictures to point to. A US children's health page for parents of toddlers, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Reading with toddlers
sources.quote: Don't worry if you can't get through a whole book. The main thing to keep in mind when reading with toddlers is that it has more to do with pointing and talking than with them sitting still and listening. ... Be willing to read only parts of a book and pages out of order ... Read when asked ... Allow your child to choose what to read whenever possible ... Toddlers rapidly develop a group of favorite books and will want you to read them again and again. ... repetition helps them to learn the meaning of words, which is vital for language development
sources.supports: No need to finish a book, pointing and talking matter more than sitting still, reading only parts or pages out of order, letting the child choose, and repeating favourite books. An Australian government parenting site, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Share Books With Your Baby
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Early Childhood (updated 29 Sep 2024)
sources.quote: Taste a book; mouthing objects like books is a normal developmental stage. ... If your baby wants to turn to a different page—just follow their lead. Remember that you never need to read the whole story. ... Babies love repetition. Don't be surprised if they like sharing the same book or certain parts of one again and again.
sources.supports: Mouthing a book at 6 to 8 months is normal, following a baby's lead to another page, never needing to read the whole story, and babies' love of repetition. The AAP's page on sharing books in the first year.

בגיל שנה ישבתי על הרצפה,
לקחתי ספר ושמתי אותו בפה.

מה יעזור לי:
שתמשיכו לקרוא, גם כשאני זז.

מה קורה לי בפנים:
אני רואה את הספרים בסל על הרצפה,

זה קצת כמו פעם,

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. Others like to look at a page or two before moving on to something else. Keep the book out — kids might want to return to it later, which you should encourage. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... Keep active hands busy with lift-the-flap pages and textures to feel. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... It's OK if your child can't sit still for an entire book — toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon. ... Choose books with many pictures that your child can point to and name.
sources.supports: Busy toddlers may stand or move while a parent reads, a child who does not look can still be listening, repeating a favourite book, a basket of books on the floor and choosing from a few, a regular time before naps and bedtime, flaps and textures for busy hands, putting the book aside when it turns tense, attention spans growing, and books with many pictures to point to. A US children's health page for parents of toddlers, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Reading with toddlers
sources.quote: Don't worry if you can't get through a whole book. The main thing to keep in mind when reading with toddlers is that it has more to do with pointing and talking than with them sitting still and listening. ... Be willing to read only parts of a book and pages out of order ... Read when asked ... Allow your child to choose what to read whenever possible ... Toddlers rapidly develop a group of favorite books and will want you to read them again and again. ... repetition helps them to learn the meaning of words, which is vital for language development
sources.supports: No need to finish a book, pointing and talking matter more than sitting still, reading only parts or pages out of order, letting the child choose, and repeating favourite books. An Australian government parenting site, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Share Books With Your Baby
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Early Childhood (updated 29 Sep 2024)
sources.quote: Taste a book; mouthing objects like books is a normal developmental stage. ... If your baby wants to turn to a different page—just follow their lead. Remember that you never need to read the whole story. ... Babies love repetition. Don't be surprised if they like sharing the same book or certain parts of one again and again.
sources.supports: Mouthing a book at 6 to 8 months is normal, following a baby's lead to another page, never needing to read the whole story, and babies' love of repetition. The AAP's page on sharing books in the first year.

sources.title: Toddler Reading Time
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Kandia N. Lewis, PhD, August 2023)
sources.quote: Some busy toddlers like to stand up while you read to them. Others like to look at a page or two before moving on to something else. Keep the book out — kids might want to return to it later, which you should encourage. ... Some kids might not look at you or the book, but that doesn't mean they're not interested or listening. ... Read whatever books your toddler asks for, even if it's the same book every night for weeks and weeks (and weeks and weeks). ... Encourage this by putting out three or four books and asking your child to pick one. ... Keep books in a basket on the floor or on a low shelf where your child can reach them and look at them by themselves. ... Choosing regular times to read (especially before naps and bedtime) helps kids learn to sit with a book and relax. ... Keep active hands busy with lift-the-flap pages and textures to feel. ... If you feel tense or your toddler resists, consider setting the book aside and returning to it later. ... It's OK if your child can't sit still for an entire book — toddlers' attention spans will get longer soon. ... Choose books with many pictures that your child can point to and name.
sources.supports: Busy toddlers may stand or move while a parent reads, a child who does not look can still be listening, repeating a favourite book, a basket of books on the floor and choosing from a few, a regular time before naps and bedtime, flaps and textures for busy hands, putting the book aside when it turns tense, attention spans growing, and books with many pictures to point to. A US children's health page for parents of toddlers, applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Reading with toddlers
sources.quote: Don't worry if you can't get through a whole book. The main thing to keep in mind when reading with toddlers is that it has more to do with pointing and talking than with them sitting still and listening. ... Be willing to read only parts of a book and pages out of order ... Read when asked ... Allow your child to choose what to read whenever possible ... Toddlers rapidly develop a group of favorite books and will want you to read them again and again. ... repetition helps them to learn the meaning of words, which is vital for language development
sources.supports: No need to finish a book, pointing and talking matter more than sitting still, reading only parts or pages out of order, letting the child choose, and repeating favourite books. An Australian government parenting site, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Share Books With Your Baby
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Early Childhood (updated 29 Sep 2024)
sources.quote: Taste a book; mouthing objects like books is a normal developmental stage. ... If your baby wants to turn to a different page—just follow their lead. Remember that you never need to read the whole story. ... Babies love repetition. Don't be surprised if they like sharing the same book or certain parts of one again and again.
sources.supports: Mouthing a book at 6 to 8 months is normal, following a baby's lead to another page, never needing to read the whole story, and babies' love of repetition. The AAP's page on sharing books in the first year.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Most children stop between two and four, talking about it a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy to hold, and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, used as general advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.quote: “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.” ... Children suck on pacifiers to self-soothe — and self-soothing is an important skill that helps them sleep. If your child is 1 or older, you can put them to bed with a light blanket or stuffed animal to help soothe them as you try to make the switch away from pacifiers. “Snuggling up with those special items offers them security and comfort throughout the night,” Dr. Sherman explains. ... Kids are motivated by praise. So, if you’re trying to convince your toddler to stop using a pacifier, be sure to tell them what a great job they’re doing of not using their pacifier.
sources.supports: A few nights of fussing and standing firm, a blanket or stuffed animal as the alternative soother, and praise. A US medical centre page, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to transition away from a dummy and bottle
sources.quote: Give your child plenty of comfort and distractions as you remove the dummy. Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Reading story books or making up a story about children that give away their dummy can help. ... Step 8: When your child only wants their dummy at bedtime. Do: Keep it in the bedroom but out of sight, remove the dummy when they are asleep, praise them for not using the dummy during the day. ... Reward your child with fun activities, stickers or bubbles, but don't give them sweets instead of their dummy.
sources.supports: Comfort and distraction while the dummy goes, a favourite blanket or toy to soothe, praise for the day without it, fun activities as a reward, and stories about children who give the dummy away. An NHS family health service page for UK families, used as general advice.

והפה שלי רוצה משהו.

״אמא!״ אני קורא
הקול שלי גדול בחושך.
אני לא כועס עלייך, אני מפחד.
הגוף שלי עוד לא יודע
איך להירדם בלי המוצץ.

את באה, בלי להדליק אור
את יושבת על קצה המיטה.
לא כועסת, ולא אומרת ״די״.
את אומרת בשקט ״אורי, אני פה.״
והקול שלך מרגיע אותי.

הדובי בא אליי
את מניחה לי אותו ביד.
הוא רך, ויש לו ריח של הכרית.
אני מחבק אותו חזק,
והבכי נהיה קטן יותר.

ובערב, לפני הלילה הבא
מה יעזור לי:
שתזכירי לי את הדובי לפני השינה,
ותגידי שאולי אתעורר שוב.
שלא תחזירי את המוצץ, גם כשאבקש.

בבוקר, תגידי לי שהצלחתי
יהיו לילות שאתעורר ואבכה.
ואחרי כל לילה, בבוקר,
תגידי לי שישנתי בלי מוצץ.
ככה אני לומד להירדם בדרך חדשה.

אפשר גם לעזור להם
עם הלילות בלי מוצץ
בעזרת ספר מותאם אישית.
תכתבי "לילה"
ואשלח לך קישור להכנת הספר 📖

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four, but you can start the process from around one year of age. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. You can talk about the replacement when they are asking for the dummy. ... Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Most children stop between two and four, talking about it a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy to hold, and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, used as general advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.quote: “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.” ... Children suck on pacifiers to self-soothe — and self-soothing is an important skill that helps them sleep. If your child is 1 or older, you can put them to bed with a light blanket or stuffed animal to help soothe them as you try to make the switch away from pacifiers. “Snuggling up with those special items offers them security and comfort throughout the night,” Dr. Sherman explains. ... Kids are motivated by praise. So, if you’re trying to convince your toddler to stop using a pacifier, be sure to tell them what a great job they’re doing of not using their pacifier.
sources.supports: A few nights of fussing and standing firm, a blanket or stuffed animal as the alternative soother, and praise. A US medical centre page, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to transition away from a dummy and bottle
sources.quote: Give your child plenty of comfort and distractions as you remove the dummy. Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Reading story books or making up a story about children that give away their dummy can help. ... Step 8: When your child only wants their dummy at bedtime. Do: Keep it in the bedroom but out of sight, remove the dummy when they are asleep, praise them for not using the dummy during the day. ... Reward your child with fun activities, stickers or bubbles, but don't give them sweets instead of their dummy.
sources.supports: Comfort and distraction while the dummy goes, a favourite blanket or toy to soothe, praise for the day without it, fun activities as a reward, and stories about children who give the dummy away. An NHS family health service page for UK families, used as general advice.
